paragraphs: Sparse recovery aims to recover a signal with relatively few active components. This paper considers settings where a graph also describes structure among those components. It introduces a flexible framework for expressing graph-based sparsity, bringing several previously studied sparsity models into a more general formulation. The contribution concerns both how to describe structured signals and how to compute with that description.

A central computational ingredient is a set of projection algorithms for the proposed model. Projection means finding a representation that fits the permitted sparsity structure. The algorithms run in nearly linear time, making this operation efficient enough to support recovery procedures rather than leaving the structural model as a purely descriptive idea.

For sparse recovery, the authors establish information-theoretically optimal sample complexity across a wide range of parameters. Within that range, the measurement requirements meet the relevant theoretical benchmark. Experiments also show improvements over prior work, providing practical evidence alongside the computational and sample-complexity results.
icml-2015-a-nearly-linear-time-framework.tldr: A flexible framework for graph-structured sparsity combines nearly linear-time projections with optimal sample complexity across a wide parameter range.

paragraphs: Multi-task feature selection learns which inputs matter across several related prediction tasks. A common assumption is that the tasks agree about which features are useful and which are irrelevant. This paper addresses exceptions to that assumption: an individual task may need a different feature set, or a particular feature may matter to only some tasks.

The authors introduce a probabilistic model with a robust prior that explicitly represents both types of exception. Binary latent variables identify outlier tasks and outlier features. These hidden indicators let the model account for departures from shared relevance instead of requiring every task and feature to follow the same pattern.

The paper uses expectation propagation for efficient approximate inference under this prior. Several experiments show better predictive performance than the benchmark methods considered. The stated result supports allowing selective exceptions to shared feature structure: related tasks can still be modeled together while accommodating differences that a stricter sharing assumption would overlook.
icml-2015-a-probabilistic-model-for-dirt.tldr: A robust probabilistic prior improves multi-task feature selection by explicitly modeling tasks and features that depart from shared relevance patterns.

paragraphs: A large graphical model may be reused for many inference questions, even when each question concerns only a small subset of its hidden variables. New measurements can also change the probabilities of interest over time. Standard belief propagation may perform unnecessary work in these settings by sending messages across the entire graph whenever inference is needed.

The paper introduces adaptive belief propagation, or AdaBP, as an inference procedure designed for these changing queries and measurements. It gives exact results on tree-structured discrete and Gaussian Markov random fields. The authors also extend the approach to Gaussian graphs with loops and to finding the most likely configuration of the entire latent graph.

Synthetic and real experiments report performance improvements of orders of magnitude over standard belief propagation. The paper also investigates when AdaBP is advantageous over another method addressing the same adaptive problem. The exactness claim is specifically established for trees; the broader contribution is an inference approach tailored to repeated, changing uses of a large model.
icml-2015-adaptive-belief-propagation-42.tldr: AdaBP accelerates inference as queries and measurements change, with exact results on discrete and Gaussian tree models.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bilinear prediction model represented by a matrix with a rank-one constraint. That constraint restricts the form of the model rather than allowing an unrestricted matrix of parameters. The authors focus on learning its parameters online, where updates are made as examples arrive, and propose an algorithm designed for this setting.

The update procedure follows the approach of online mirror descent, with gradients computed using power iteration. These ingredients connect the online learning rule to the matrix structure of the model. The paper therefore supplies a concrete training procedure for the constrained predictor, rather than only describing the model or its possible uses.

To analyze the algorithm, the authors develop a second-order approximation to the squared spectral norm and use it to obtain a regret bound. Regret measures accumulated performance relative to a comparison predictor. Experiments on two sequential labeling tasks give positive results, complementing the theoretical analysis without establishing a broader claim of superiority across all online prediction problems.
icml-2015-an-online-learning-algorithm-f.tldr: An online mirror-descent-style algorithm trains rank-one bilinear models using power iteration and comes with a regret bound.

paragraphs: An ensemble of decision trees combines multiple trees into a predictive model. This paper derives such ensembles from a nonparametric Bayesian model, allowing the trees to be interpreted as samples from a posterior distribution. That interpretation gives the ensemble a probabilistic basis and motivates a class of algorithms called Bayesian Forests.

The authors report small predictive performance gains and large improvements in interpretability for these algorithms. Within the same framework, they show that the high-level tree hierarchy becomes stable in large samples. This result concerns the broad organization of the trees and provides a reason to exploit that organization when constructing forests at larger scales.

The stability finding motivates Empirical Bayesian Forests, an approximate approach intended for massive datasets distributed across machines. The paper reports that these forests outperform alternatives based on subsampling by a large margin. The contributions therefore connect an interpretable Bayesian account of tree ensembles with a computational strategy for building approximate versions on distributed data.
icml-2015-bayesian-and-empirical-bayesia.tldr: A Bayesian interpretation of tree ensembles motivates more interpretable forests and a scalable approximation for massive distributed datasets.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization automates the search for useful model hyperparameters. When the data used to evaluate those choices are sensitive, the optimization outputs can themselves expose information about the data. This paper focuses on that release step: how to disclose the selected hyperparameters and classifier accuracy while providing differential privacy.

The authors develop private release methods and analyze their usefulness by combining differential privacy guarantees with known convergence bounds for Bayesian optimization. Under a Gaussian process assumption, they prove that the privately released quantities are often near-optimal. The result links protection of the tuning data to the quality of the information practitioners receive.

The Gaussian process assumption matters to the stated near-optimality result. The paper also explains how other smoothness guarantees can protect privacy when that assumption does not hold. This distinguishes the conditions used to establish output quality from the alternative conditions available for privacy protection, while addressing the practical need to report useful results from sensitive model-tuning data.
icml-2015-differentially-private-bayesia.tldr: Private Bayesian optimization releases selected hyperparameters and accuracy with privacy guarantees and conditional near-optimality results.

paragraphs: Training a linear support vector machine can require more data than a single machine can hold. This paper addresses distributed training through the model's dual optimization problem, a quadratic objective with bounds on its variables. The goal is to make progress toward the solution efficiently while coordinating computation across machines.

The central contribution is an analytical way to compute the optimal step size at each iteration. Its communication cost is O(1), so this particular calculation requires only constant communication. The step-size result is paired with a global linear convergence guarantee even though the linear SVM dual problem is not strongly convex.

Linear convergence means the iteration requirement grows as O(log(1/ε)) for an ε-accurate solution. This gives a precise account of how the method approaches higher accuracy. Experiments also report substantially faster training than the distributed SVM algorithms compared in the paper. Together, the results connect a low-communication step-size calculation to both a convergence guarantee and observed training speed.
icml-2015-distributed-box-constrained-qu.tldr: An optimal step-size calculation with constant communication enables globally linearly convergent distributed training of linear SVMs.

paragraphs: In a combinatorial semi-bandit problem, an agent repeatedly chooses a permitted subset of items. It observes the random weights of the selected items and receives their sum as its payoff. The challenge is to learn which combinations are valuable while respecting the constraints on selection, especially when the number of available items is large.

The paper introduces Combinatorial Linear Thompson Sampling and Combinatorial Linear UCB for this setting with linear generalization. Both are computationally efficient provided the corresponding offline combinatorial problem can be solved efficiently. Their computational claim therefore depends on the underlying selection problem being tractable.

Under the stated assumptions, the authors derive regret bounds that are independent of the number of items and sublinear in time. These bounds establish statistical efficiency as learning proceeds. Experiments with thousands of items evaluate the Thompson sampling method, reporting scalability, robustness to parameter choices, and substantial improvements over the strongest tested baseline. The empirical findings concern that algorithm, while the theoretical results cover both.
icml-2015-efficient-learning-in-large-sc.tldr: Two algorithms learn constrained item selections with item-count-independent regret bounds and computational efficiency when offline selection is tractable.

paragraphs: When uncertainty is central to a Gaussian process application, the model must account for uncertainty in its covariance parameters. This paper targets their posterior distribution rather than treating a single parameter setting as sufficient. It adapts Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics to draw posterior samples with negligible bias without computing the marginal likelihood.

For Gaussian process regression, this formulation allows stochastic gradients to be calculated through linear-system solves alone. The authors introduce ULISSE, an unbiased linear-system solver, to accelerate unbiased gradient estimation. Its core computations are covariance matrix-vector products, which can be parallelized.

The results demonstrate the possibility of scalable uncertainty quantification that is exact in a Monte Carlo sense. The approach does not require special covariance structure or a reduction in the number of input vectors. These qualifications distinguish the contribution: it changes the computations used for posterior sampling while retaining the full set of inputs, with exactness understood in the sampling sense and the adapted procedure described as having negligible bias.
icml-2015-enabling-scalable-stochastic-g.tldr: ULISSE accelerates Gaussian process posterior sampling through unbiased linear-system solves without requiring structured covariances or fewer inputs.

paragraphs: The paper develops an automated method for detecting damped Lyman-alpha absorbers along spectroscopic sightlines to quasars. Finding these absorbers in large spectroscopic surveys is important for investigating cosmological questions, including galaxy formation. The research addresses the detection problem at survey scale, where a method must work across large collections of spectra.

The authors learn a Gaussian process model tailored to quasar emission spectra using nearly 50,000 spectra. They then use Bayesian model selection to apply that learned model to absorber detection. This connects a statistical description of quasar emission to a probabilistic decision about the presence of an absorber in an observed spectrum.

A validation experiment on more than 100,000 spectra demonstrates the method's effectiveness, with performance described as excellent. The stated finding is evidence for automated detection on a large spectral collection. The contribution combines a learned emission model, Bayesian model selection, and large-scale validation to support the observational work needed for the broader cosmological questions.
icml-2015-finding-galaxies-in-the-shadow.tldr: A Gaussian process model learned from quasar spectra enables automated absorber detection through Bayesian model selection.

paragraphs: Online structured prediction involves making a sequence of decisions whose outputs have internal structure. This paper investigates a new Follow the Perturbed Leader algorithm for such problems. Its analysis centers on regret, which measures the accumulated cost of the learner's decisions relative to a comparison choice over the same sequence.

The authors prove a regret bound comparable to existing leading FTPL bounds and, in some cases, comparable to the best achievable regret. They also establish a lower bound for a broad, natural class of FTPL algorithms using logconcave perturbations. This second result helps characterize the limits of that algorithmic class alongside the performance guarantee for the new method.

An online shortest-path experiment provides an empirical test involving structured decisions. The results show both statistical and computational efficiency in that setting. The paper thus combines an algorithm, an upper bound on its regret, and a lower bound for a related class, while reserving the strongest comparison to optimal regret for the cases where it applies.
icml-2015-following-the-perturbed-leader.tldr: A new FTPL algorithm offers competitive regret for online structured prediction, alongside a lower bound for algorithms with logconcave perturbations.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Word Mover's Distance, a way to compare documents using word representations that capture semantic relationships. Those representations are learned from words appearing near one another in sentences. The method uses the geometry of this embedding space to define document dissimilarity, connecting word-level meaning to a distance between whole texts.

The distance is the minimum total travel needed to move the embedded words of one document onto those of another. The authors formulate this as an Earth Mover's Distance problem, connecting document comparison to an established transportation problem with efficient solvers. The proposed metric has no hyperparameters and is described as straightforward to implement.

The authors evaluate the distance through nearest-neighbor document classification on eight real-world datasets against seven leading baselines. They report exceptionally low classification error rates in those comparisons. These findings show that the proposed transportation-based measure can make document proximity useful for classification, translating the semantic organization of word embeddings into a practical document-level comparison.
icml-2015-from-word-embeddings-to-docume.tldr: Word Mover's Distance compares documents by the minimum transportation cost between their embedded words.

paragraphs: Graph inference asks whether the connections of an unknown network can be recovered by observing cascades that spread across it. This paper treats that task as sparse recovery. The relevant structural quantity is the maximum number of neighbors of a node, allowing the analysis to express recovery requirements in terms of graph sparsity.

The authors introduce a general cascade model that includes both the voter model and the independent cascade model. For this setting, their algorithm recovers graph edges with high probability using O(s log m) measurements, where s is the maximum degree and m is the number of nodes. It also recovers edge weights governing diffusion and remains robust under approximate sparsity.

An almost matching lower bound shows that the measurement requirement is close to a fundamental limit in the analyzed setting. Experiments on synthetic graphs validate the approach empirically. Together, these results address both which connections exist and how strongly diffusion operates along them, with recovery stated probabilistically rather than as an unconditional guarantee.
icml-2015-inferring-graphs-from-cascades.tldr: A sparse-recovery approach infers graph edges and diffusion weights from cascades with near-optimal measurement requirements.

paragraphs: Log-determinants appear in many machine learning computations, including Gaussian models and kernel learning. A standard Cholesky-based calculation has cubic cost in matrix dimension, which becomes prohibitive for very large matrices. This paper develops a randomized approximation approach for large positive definite and general nonsingular matrices.

The algorithm combines Hutchinson stochastic trace estimation with Chebyshev polynomial expansions. Both components rely on efficient matrix-vector multiplication, replacing the need for the expensive decomposition used by the standard calculation. The proposed linear-time approach therefore centers on operations that can be practical even when a full matrix factorization is too costly.

The authors prove additive and multiplicative error bounds that depend on the input matrix's condition number. Their experiments show that very accurate approximations can be obtained orders of magnitude faster than the compared decomposition methods, and demonstrate computations involving tens of millions of variables. The contribution couples large-scale computational savings with explicit approximation guarantees whose strength depends on matrix conditioning.
icml-2015-large-scale-log-determinant-co.tldr: Randomized trace estimation and Chebyshev expansions approximate large-matrix log-determinants efficiently with conditioning-dependent error bounds.

paragraphs: Markov decision problems become expensive to solve when their state spaces are large. The computational effort and statistical requirements of finding an optimal policy both grow with that space. This paper studies average-cost and total-cost problems by restricting the search to a low-dimensional family of policies, aiming for a strong policy within that family.

For problems with a Kullback-Leibler divergence cost function, the authors show how to turn policy optimization into a convex optimization problem. They then solve it approximately with a stochastic subgradient algorithm. The particular cost structure is central to this reduction, which provides a tractable route to searching the restricted policy family.

The resulting policy is shown to perform close to the best policy in that low-dimensional family. This comparison defines the scope of the near-optimality result. An application to allocating budgets for crowdsourced labeling demonstrates the approach's effectiveness, connecting the theoretical optimization framework to a concrete sequential resource-allocation task.
icml-2015-large-scale-markov-decision-pr.tldr: KL control costs enable convex optimization of a restricted policy family, with performance close to the best policy in that family.

paragraphs: Learning methods sometimes use Markov Chain Monte Carlo to approximate the inference calculations needed during training. If the chain mixes slowly, its samples may poorly represent the distribution being estimated. The resulting approximate gradients can damage learning, and the paper emphasizes that slow mixing itself can be difficult to diagnose.

The authors address this problem by defining a model family through strong Doeblin Markov chains. A parameter precisely controls the mixing time of these chains. This makes mixing behavior part of the model's design, giving the learning procedure explicit control over a property that otherwise can undermine its inference calculations.

The accompanying learning algorithm maximizes the data likelihood under the stationary distribution induced by the chain. In this formulation, the distribution used to model the data is directly linked to the chain whose mixing is controlled. Experiments show improvements on two challenging inference tasks, supporting the practical value of this connection between model construction, inference behavior, and likelihood-based learning.
icml-2015-learning-fast-mixing-models-fo.tldr: A model family built from strong Doeblin chains makes mixing time controllable and supports likelihood-based learning.

paragraphs: Open-ended programming assignments create a difficult feedback problem in classes with thousands or millions of students. Instructors need to assess completed work and help students who are stuck, but individual attention is hard to provide at that scale. This paper develops a learned program representation to support the distribution of feedback across many submissions.

The neural network method represents a program as a linear mapping from an embedded precondition space to an embedded postcondition space. In other words, its representation relates conditions before the program to conditions after it. The authors then use these linear maps as features in an algorithm for providing feedback at scale.

The method is applied to assessments from Code.org's Hour of Code and Stanford's introductory computer science course. In these applications, human comments are propagated to orders of magnitude more submissions. The stated achievement is a substantial expansion in the reach of existing human feedback, using learned program representations to support its reuse across student work.
icml-2015-learning-program-embeddings-to.tldr: Learned program representations let human feedback reach orders of magnitude more student submissions.

paragraphs: MADE turns an autoencoder into a model that assigns probabilities to complete inputs. The key change is to mask network parameters so that each input component is reconstructed using only earlier components in a chosen ordering. This restriction gives the network the dependency structure needed for an autoregressive probability model.

With those dependencies enforced, each output represents a conditional probability, and multiplying the conditionals gives the joint probability of the input. The authors also show how a single network can support multiple orderings. Their framework applies to several network architectures, including deep networks, so the construction is not tied to one shallow design.

The masking approach supports simple, fast vectorized implementations, including on GPUs. Experiments find it competitive with leading tractable distribution estimators, while test-time computation is significantly faster and scales better than other autoregressive estimators. The contribution is therefore both a probabilistic reinterpretation of a familiar network and an implementation approach with demonstrated computational advantages.
icml-2015-made-masked-autoencoder-for-di.tldr: MADE masks autoencoder connections to produce a fast autoregressive probability model with competitive density-estimation performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies representation learning when multiple unlabeled views of the same data are available during learning, but only one view will be available at test time. The task is to use the richer training information to learn features that remain useful under that restricted test-time setting.

The authors analyze and compare several deep-network approaches from prior work along with new variants. The methods include autoencoder-style networks trained through reconstruction and paired feedforward networks trained through correlation objectives. Evaluations span visual, speech, and language tasks, creating a direct comparison of approaches across multiple domains rather than relying on results from separate studies.

The comparisons favor correlation-based representation learning. A new variant, deep canonically correlated autoencoders, achieves the best results on most of the evaluated tasks. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is broad within these experiments but is not stated for every task. The paper contributes both comparative evidence about training objectives and a new method that performs particularly well in the tested setting.
icml-2015-on-deep-multi-view-representat.tldr: A comparison across visual, speech, and language tasks favors correlation-based features, with DCCAE performing best on most tasks.

paragraphs: The paper identifies an equivalence for linear classifiers: minimizing logistic loss on examples is equivalent to minimizing an exponential loss on transformed data called Rademacher observations, or rados. Both objectives use the same classifier. Consequently, a classifier learned from rados can be applied directly to ordinary observations.

The authors develop a learning algorithm over rados with boosting-compatible convergence rates measured on the original examples' logistic loss. Experiments involving up to millions of examples, supported by theoretical arguments, show that learning from a small random collection of rados can compete with leading methods using the complete example set.

The paper also examines privacy through algebraic, geometric, and computational-hardness results about reconstructing examples from rados. Beyond those properties, it shows how to construct rados and learn from them efficiently within a differential privacy framework. Tests reveal meaningful privacy–accuracy tradeoffs. The learning equivalence and the privacy constructions are complementary contributions: transformed observations support prediction, while the specific private construction provides differential privacy.
icml-2015-rademacher-observations-privat.tldr: Rademacher observations support equivalent linear-classifier learning objectives and enable privacy-aware learning with measurable accuracy tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Graphical modeling often presents a tension between simple models with exact inference and expressive models that require approximate inference. Expressivity can improve accuracy, while coverage of the possible outcomes matters for confidence estimation and learning from indirect supervision. This paper introduces reified context models to bring these desirable properties together.

The central idea is to make the choice of factors in a graphical model a set of random variables within the model itself. These choices are the contexts. Making them explicit allows the model to choose contexts in a data-dependent way, so the structure used to represent a situation becomes part of the probabilistic modeling process.

Experiments on three sequence-modeling tasks show that the approach obtains both expressivity and coverage. The contribution is thus a modeling mechanism for addressing the inference–expressivity tension, supported by evidence from those tasks. Its distinctive move is to represent contextual choices inside the model, allowing their selection to depend on the data being modeled.
icml-2015-reified-context-models-01c0514.tldr: Reified context models treat factor choices as random variables, enabling data-dependent contexts that combine expressivity and coverage.

paragraphs: Optimizing an unknown function from noisy observations requires choosing where to gather information and where to pursue promising outcomes. Some applications add a stricter requirement: every sampled function value must stay above a specified safety threshold. This paper studies that requirement as part of sequential optimization, rather than judging a method only by the final value it finds.

The authors introduce SafeOpt under regularity assumptions expressed through a Gaussian process prior. The algorithm addresses exploration and optimization together with the safety constraint. Their theoretical result guarantees convergence to a notion of optimum that is reachable under those constraints, making safe reachability part of the objective being analyzed.

This reachable optimum is the relevant target because the safety requirement constrains which evaluations the procedure can make. The paper evaluates SafeOpt on synthetic data and in movie recommendation and therapeutic spinal cord stimulation. These applications illustrate the intended setting: learning useful decisions while respecting a threshold throughout the process, under the assumptions supporting the analysis.
icml-2015-safe-exploration-for-optimizat.tldr: SafeOpt optimizes from noisy observations under a safety threshold, with conditional convergence to a safely reachable optimum.

paragraphs: Nuclear norm regularization encourages low-rank matrix solutions, but optimization can still become expensive when the matrix variables are large. This paper introduces safe subspace screening for nuclear-norm-regularized least squares. Its purpose is to shrink the optimization problem before an existing solver begins its main work.

The approach uses the fact that a low-rank solution can be represented through relatively few subspaces. It identifies and discards a large proportion of inactive subspaces, leaving a smaller problem to solve. The screening is safe in the stated sense that the resulting solution is identical to the solution obtained by the solver on the original problem.

Because screening is independent of the solver, the authors state that it can be combined with any existing nuclear norm solver. Experiments on several synthetic and real datasets demonstrate effective removal of inactive subspaces. The contribution is a way to reduce computational burden while preserving the solution, making the preprocessing step useful alongside existing optimization methods.
icml-2015-safe-subspace-screening-for-nu.tldr: Safe subspace screening reduces nuclear-norm least-squares problems before optimization while preserving the solver's solution.

paragraphs: Some classification inputs, including EEG measurements and images, naturally take matrix form. Relationships among their rows or columns can carry useful information. This paper proposes the support matrix machine to incorporate that structure into classification, with particular attention to correlations among groups of matrix features.

The method combines hinge loss with a spectral elastic net penalty, a matrix-oriented extension of the conventional elastic net. The penalty has a grouping effect: strongly correlated rows or columns tend to be selected together or excluded together. This gives the classifier a way to reflect the relatedness of features when determining which matrix structure matters.

The resulting optimization problem is convex, and the authors develop an alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm to solve it. Experiments on EEG and face-image classification report greater robustness and efficiency than the leading methods considered. These findings support the practical value of combining matrix-aware regularization with a convex classification objective on the evaluated data.
icml-2015-support-matrix-machines-fd86c6.tldr: Support matrix machines use a convex matrix-aware penalty that tends to select correlated rows or columns together.

paragraphs: A competition leaderboard repeatedly evaluates submissions using held-out data. Because participants adapt later submissions to earlier scores, they can gradually overfit that data. This paper asks how a leaderboard can continue to represent the quality of each team's best submission accurately despite this feedback loop.

The authors define an accuracy criterion tailored to leaderboards and introduce the Ladder algorithm. They establish strong theoretical guarantees in a fully adaptive estimation setting. The choice of criterion is consequential: it allows them to avoid a hardness result that would prohibit such algorithms under a different, seemingly similar definition of adaptive estimation accuracy.

The evaluation shows resistance to practical adversarial attacks and high utility on actual submission files from a Kaggle competition. The paper also supplies a parameter-free variant intended for deployment without tuning. Together, these contributions provide a theoretically grounded way to maintain useful competition feedback, with practical evidence supporting its reliability under adaptive use.
icml-2015-the-ladder-a-reliable-leaderbo.tldr: The Ladder maintains reliable competition feedback under adaptive submissions using a leaderboard-specific accuracy criterion.
